wrapTickLabel = (label, maxWidth = 10) => {
  if (!label || label.length <= maxWidth) return label;
  const words = label.split(" ");
  const lines = [];
  let currentLine = "";
  for (const word of words) {
    if ((currentLine + " " + word).trim().length <= maxWidth) {
      currentLine = (currentLine + " " + word).trim();
    } else {
      if (currentLine) lines.push(currentLine);
      currentLine = word;
    }
  }
  if (currentLine) lines.push(currentLine);
  return lines.join("\n");
}

START HERE • USER GUIDE & PHYSICAL TELECONNECTIONS

Section 0 • How to Use the Kenya ENSO Explorer

An empirical climate intelligence and decision-support system linking large-scale equatorial ocean dynamics (Pacific ENSO, Indian Ocean Dipole, and Western Pacific Gradient) to county-level agricultural production, rangeland forage resilience, flood inundation, and humanitarian emergency vulnerability across Kenya's 47 counties.

Statutory Authority & Forecast Boundary: The ENSO Explorer is an empirical research and risk assessment platform designed for climate rationale development, long-term contingency planning, and adaptation financing. It is NOT an operational daily weather forecast or statutory seasonal warning. For official, binding meteorological advisories and early warnings in Kenya, consult the statutory authorities: the Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) at meteo.go.ke and the IGAD Climate Prediction & Applications Centre (ICPAC) at icpac.net.

Three-Step Decision Workflow for County Officials & Proposal Writers

Follow this structured path to translate planetary climate signals into actionable county investment priorities and defensible adaptation finance rationales (GCF, AF, GEF, CIDP).

1

Select County & Season

Use the sticky control toolbar above to choose your target county and primary agricultural season (OND Short Rains or MAM Long Rains). Inspect Section 1 to review statutory KNBS crop and livestock baselines, modeled production value, and multi-dimensional vulnerability rankings.

2

Inspect Seasonal Outlook

Check the live NOAA CPC equatorial ocean state probabilities and view the top historical analogue seasons ranked by Euclidean distance in joint ocean-temperature space. Examine empirical tercile shifts and multi-hazard outcomes from the most similar historical seasons.

3

Review Historical Evidence

Examine 44-year CHIRPS rainfall distributions, satellite raster history (NDVI, SAR flood, WRSI), and audited KNBS harvest shocks across past ocean states. Build empirical causal baselines that satisfy donor review standards without relying on ungrounded assumptions.

Understanding Kenya's Planetary Teleconnections in Plain Language

Kenya's bimodal rainfall is governed by three distinct ocean and atmospheric teleconnection engines operating across thousands of miles of tropical ocean.

ENSO (Pacific Ocean)

RONI Index

El Niño–Southern Oscillation: The warming (El Niño) and cooling (La Niña) of surface waters across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific. In Kenya, El Niño shifts the atmospheric Walker circulation, strongly favoring above-normal rainfall during the OND Short Rains (flood risk), whereas La Niña strongly favors severe drought.

Governing metric: Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI)

IOD (Indian Ocean)

DMI Index

Indian Ocean Dipole: An east-west temperature see-saw across the equatorial Indian Ocean. A Positive IOD (+IOD) warms the western Indian Ocean near Kenya, pumping vast moisture inland. When a +IOD co-occurs with El Niño (as in 1997, 2006, 2019, and 2023), it causes historic mega-floods. Negative IOD (-IOD) exacerbates drought.

Governing metric: Dipole Mode Index (DMI)

Western-V (Western Pacific)

WNP Metric

Western Pacific Gradient: A sea-surface temperature and convective gradient across the Western North Pacific that drives East Africa's MAM Long Rains. During MAM, canonical Pacific ENSO correlations decouple across Kenya, and the Western-V mode takes precedence in modulating monsoon onset and moisture transport.

Governing metric: Western North Pacific anomaly (WNP)
Spatial & Seasonal Regime Notice: Why "One Rule for Kenya" Fails

While El Niño brings surplus moisture to northern pastoral ASALs (Marsabit, Wajir, Garissa) and eastern lowlands during OND, western Kenya (Lake Victoria basin, Trans Nzoia, Uasin Gishu) follows a distinct rainfall regime with substantial June–August (JJA) rainfall governed by Congo moisture fluxes. Always examine county-specific climatology (Section 1) rather than applying national generalizations.

Sub-County Administrative, Demographic & Climatological Baseline — Marsabit (4 Sub-counties)

Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Data Sources & Legal Mandate

Geographic land area, population headcounts, and administrative ward boundaries are established under the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) 2019 Kenya Population & Housing Census (Volume I & Volume IV) and the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) statutory gazette.

Processing & Spatial Harmonization
  • Spatial Boundary Aggregation: County and sub-county administrative polygons are standardized to Global Administrative Unit Layers (GAUL) 2024 Level 1 and Level 2 geometry. Surface areas are calculated via an Albers Equal Area Conic projection (EPSG:102022) to avoid equatorial planar distortion.
  • Dominant Season Derivation & Equimodal Regimes: Seasonality classification is derived from the 30-year CHIRPS v3 (1991–2020) WMO climatological baseline. Sub-counties are classified into three distinct physical rainfall regimes:
    • Bimodal (Equimodal): Where MAM and OND seasonal accumulations differ by less than 25 mm or each season accounts for 45%–55% of the total bimodal volume (e.g. Saku in Marsabit: 289.7 mm MAM vs. 279.0 mm OND, 50.9% vs. 49.1%). In these balanced transition zones, neither season overwhelms the other, and pastoral forage replenishment depends critically on both rainfall windows.
    • MAM (Long Rains): Where MAM accounts for >55% of bimodal rainfall and exceeds OND by at least 25 mm (characteristic of western Kenya, central highlands, and Rift Valley).
    • OND (Short Rains): Where OND accounts for >55% of bimodal rainfall and exceeds MAM by at least 25 mm (characteristic of eastern pastoral lowlands including Garissa, Wajir, Mandera, and Tana River).
  • 2026 Population Projections: Official sub-county 2026 population projections are not available from an approved statutory source. Multilateral project filings (GCF, AF, GEF, CIDPs) must cite official KNBS 2019 Census counts rather than speculative extrapolations.
  • Proposal & Finance Alignment: County demographics and surface area figures align directly with the Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA) Third Basis for Revenue Sharing formula and statutory County Integrated Development Plans (CIDPs).

Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Data Sources & Ingestion Pipeline

Official county production statistics are extracted from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) National Agricultural Produce Reports (NAPR 2019–2024 editions), Agriculture and Food Authority (AFA) rice statistics, and the 2019 Kenya Population & Housing Census Volume IV (Distribution of Population by Socio-Economic Characteristics).

Audit Trail & Reconciliation Protocol
  • Dual-Engine Extraction: Official published report tables were extracted via dual PDF table engines (PyMuPDF and pdfplumber) with character-level coordinate verification and automated OCR cross-checks.
  • National Additivity Reconciliation: For every crop and livestock species, sub-national county values are audited against published national totals to ensure the sum of counties equals the statutory national figure within ±0.05% rounding tolerance.
  • Crucial Protocol: Blank ≠ Zero: An unsurveyed county or commodity in a specific reporting cycle is coded as missing (NaN / ∅ marker), NOT zero. A reported zero denotes an active survey recording zero yield. For arid rangeland counties (e.g., Marsabit, Turkana), rainfed crop farming is concentrated in isolated agro-pastoral sub-counties (e.g. Mount Marsabit / Saku); missing years reflect non-surveyed cycles rather than complete crop failure.
  • Statutory Alignment: These audited administrative statistics carry binding statutory authority under Kenyan law and form the mandatory baseline for CIDP sector plans and multilateral funding proposals (GCF, AF, GEF).

Figure 1.2

Spatially Modeled Value of Production Portfolio (IFPRI MapSPAM & FAO GLW4) — Marsabit

Gross agricultural capital portfolio in nominal 2021 USD (vop_nominal-usd21; undeflated) modeled via IFPRI MapSPAM (1 km crops) and FAO GLW4 (1 km livestock).

Methodological Boundary & Valuation Caveats: MapSPAM and GLW4 provide downscaled econometric distributions expressed on a Nominal 2021 USD basis (vop_nominal-usd21; undeflated). Because values are undeflated, cross-timeframe comparisons conflate macroeconomic price inflation with physical hazard shifts. While downscaled using global spatial priors, both layers are anchored to national agricultural census baselines (IFPRI MapSPAM 2020 v1r2 and FAO GLW4 2015 normalized to 2021 FAOSTAT producer prices), ensuring alignment with official national totals. Furthermore, note an open pipeline defect: livestock currently fails its national FAOSTAT reconciliation gate at a ratio of 1.198 (tracked in hazards_prototype#30). These modeled totals remain essential for demonstrating to international donors that livestock represents 90%–97% of agricultural wealth in pastoral ASALs (directing adaptation finance proportionally to pastoral resilience while safeguarding vital highland agro-pastoral cropping sanctuaries like Saku and Moyale). However, because they are modeled from global priors, they must not be cited as subcounty administrative census statistics. Use Section 1.1 for legal administrative census numbers.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Data Sources & Modeling Prior

Crop capital distributions are modeled from the IFPRI Spatial Production Allocation Model (MapSPAM 2020 v1r2) at 1 km resolution. Livestock capital distributions are downscaled from the FAO Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW4) at 1 km resolution, disaggregated across cattle, sheep, goats, and camels.

Econometric Normalization & Scope
  • Nominal Currency Basis (vop_nominal-usd21): All production outputs and herd headcounts are monetized into Nominal 2021 USD (undeflated) using FAOSTAT 2021 producer prices. Because this series is undeflated, multi-year comparisons mix macroeconomic price inflation with climate hazard shifts.
  • Open Calibration Defect (hazards_prototype#30): In the upstream processing pipeline, livestock currently fails its national FAOSTAT reconciliation gate at a ratio of 1.198 (modeled aggregate exceeds FAOSTAT national total by ~20%). Users should treat absolute dollar totals as indicative orders of magnitude while the upstream calibration is refined.
  • Spatial Zonal Aggregation: 1 km grid cells are zonal-summed over official Kenya county boundary vectors to establish gross agricultural capital endowments.
  • Spatial Nuance: In arid rangelands (e.g., Marsabit, Turkana, Wajir, Mandera), rainfed field cropping is not uniformly spread; it is clustered in highland agro-pastoral pockets (e.g. Saku and Moyale in Marsabit) or irrigated river corridors.
  • Strategic Financing Role: In pastoral ASAL counties, pastoralist herds represent 90%–97% of agricultural Value of Production (VoP). This establishes the macroeconomic evidence required by GCF and Adaptation Fund investment boards to prioritize rangeland water retention, index-based livestock insurance (IBLI), and veterinary cold chains over unviable crop irrigation schemes.

Why this data & analysis? Statutory Legitimacy

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Climate project proposals (GCF, GEF, Adaptation Fund) frequently fail donor review because they rely on modelled or unverified third-party socio-economic indicators. We exclusively use the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) 2019 National Population & Housing Census and 2023 County Gender Data Sheets. These are Kenya's official legal statistics used by the Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA).

Key Assumptions
  • Structural Baseline: Multi-dimensional poverty headcounts and household structures are assumed to represent decadal vulnerability baselines that exacerbate climate shock sensitivity.
  • Census Coverage: County totals are pegged directly to the official KNBS census gazetteer, with 100% additivity across all 47 counties.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Inter-Censal Drifts: Changes occurring post-2019 (e.g., population displacement following the 2020–2023 drought) are not reflected in static census tables.
  • Intra-County Heterogeneity: County-level averages mask acute disparities between urban county headquarters (e.g. Saku) and remote pastoral wards (e.g. North Horr).
Primary Source: KNBS 2019 Census • KNBS 2023 County Gender Data Sheets • data/KE-enso-explorer/gesi_v2.parquet

2 • Outlook & Scenario Preparedness

Section 2 • Seasonal Outlook & Preparedness — Marsabit

Live ocean driver telemetry, official KMSA/NOAA seasonal projections, and nearest historical analogue preparedness scenarios.

Operational Purpose: This section equips county directors, disaster risk committees, and development partners to anchor anticipatory action in empirical physical evidence. It supports pre-season contingency budgeting, seed distribution (drought-tolerant cereals vs waterlogging-tolerant varieties), livestock disease ring-vaccination, and borehole/culvert clearing before seasonal rains commence.
The Three-Tier Early Warning Architecture:
1. Ocean Teleconnection Forcing
Global equatorial Pacific (RONI) and Indian Ocean Dipole (DMI) sea surface temperature configurations. Sets planetary boundary conditions; does not constitute a localized rainfall forecast.
2. Seasonal Rainfall Outlook
Empirical tercile probability distributions conditioned on matched historical analogues (Figure 2.1). Official seasonal forecasts and 7-day county advisories are legally issued exclusively by KMSA.
3. Forward Impact Scenarios
End-to-end historical analogue scenarios (Figure 2.2) demonstrating how multi-hazard shocks (crop deficits, pasture crashes, floods, and market Terms of Trade deterioration) propagated during matched ocean years.
Official Governance & Statutory Alignment

Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA) Statutory Framework

Pursuant to the Meteorology Act No. 7 of 2026 (assented March 13, 2026), the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA; official products may retain Kenya Meteorological Department/KMD branding during transition) is the statutory designated authority legally mandated to formulate, issue, and regulate all official weather forecasts, seasonal climate outlooks, and operational early warning advisories in the Republic of Kenya.

Mandate Boundary & Platform Role: The Adaptation Atlas does not produce independent operational forecasts or issue unilateral disaster directives. It provides historical analogue scenarios and teleconnection risk diagnostics. County governments, disaster committees, and development partners must strictly anchor all operational triggers and contingency funding to official KMSA bulletins and localized advisories from County Directors of Meteorology (CDMs).
Figure 2.1

Short Rains (OND) Empirical Tercile Probabilities & Analogue Matching

What is the empirical probability of a wetter, near-normal, or drier season across Kenya conditioned on nearest historical ocean analogues, and how do scenarios shift when matching lead-in months vs. the projected season?

Calculating empirical tercile probabilities across nearest analogue seasons...
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this analogue method? Empirical Conditioning

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Dynamic numerical climate models often exhibit systematic rainfall biases over East Africa's complex terrain. Evaluating empirical historical analogues with matched equatorial Pacific (RONI) and Indian Ocean (DMI) sea surface temperature configurations grounds scenarios in observed physical reality.

Key Assumptions
  • Standardized Metric Space: Z-scoring applied (σRONI=1.179, σDMI=0.362) to prevent RONI from exerting 10.6× artificial leverage over DMI.
  • Detrending: Linear warming trends removed to isolate interannual teleconnection forcing from secular climate change.
Caveats & Limitations
  • No Two Events Are Identical: Atmospheric noise and Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) intra-seasonal pulses can modulate outcomes.
  • KMSA Operational Precedence: Statutory operational planning requires official KMSA seasonal forecast confirmation.
Primary Source: NOAA CPC ERSSTv6 • NOAA CPC / HadISST DMI • CHIRPS v3
MAM Teleconnection

Long Rains (MAM) Boundary & Western-V Dynamics

Why Pacific ENSO forecasts have near-zero skill for March–May in Kenya.

A common institutional mistake is applying El Niño or La Niña forecasts to Kenya's Long Rains (MAM). In equatorial East Africa, Pacific ENSO skill drops close to zero during the boreal spring predictability barrier:

Physical Mechanisms Driving MAM Rainfall:
  • The Western-V SST Gradient: Differential warming between the western Pacific and Indian Ocean steers localized subsidence over Kenya (Funk et al., 2019).
  • Regional Air-Sea Interaction: Localized moisture convergence from the Congo Basin and southwestern Indian Ocean dominates over distant ENSO signals.
  • Operational Guidance: For MAM planning, county directors must consult KMSA downscaled March–May outlooks rather than global ENSO news trackers.

Why Analogue Multi-Hazard Diagnostics? Empirical Grounding

Single-variable rainfall forecasts fail to capture compound hazard transmission. By coupling historical ocean states with satellite-derived pasture vegetative flushes (MODIS NDVI) and pastoral grain exchange rates (FEWS NET/NDMA Terms of Trade), county directors can evaluate how previous analogous seasons impacted food security, livestock markets, and emergency response budgets.

Key Assumptions
  • Standardized Predictor Space: Nearest neighbours are ranked using normalized Euclidean distance in joint RONI + DMI space.
  • Two-Season Memory: Pasture and livestock conditions depend heavily on whether the preceding MAM Long Rains were wet or dry.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Market Context: Terms of trade reflect historical commodity price regimes and macro inflation that may differ from current economic baselines.
  • Local Variations: Micro-climates and intra-seasonal dry spells can modulate local outcomes even in wet analogue years.
Primary Source: NOAA CPC ERSSTv6 • CHIRPS v3 • MODIS NDVI • NDMA / FEWS NET

Table 2.2

Official Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA) Seasonal Sectoral Advisory Matrix

Transcribed verbatim from official seasonal bulletins issued by the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA) (formerly KMD) in liaison with the Ministry of Agriculture & Livestock Development, Ministry of Water, Sanitation & Irrigation, National Drought Management Authority (NDMA), and Kenya Red Cross Society (KRCS).

meteo.go.ke Seasonal Forecasts → meteo.go.ke National Portal →
Release Cadence & Operational Sourcing: Sourced directly from official seasonal releases: The October–November–December (OND) Seasonal Climate Outlook and Potential Socio-Economic Impacts (Ref: KMD/FCST/SO Series) and The March–April–May (MAM) Seasonal Climate Outlook. Bulletins are published bi-annually (late August / early September for OND Short Rains; late February for MAM Long Rains). County-specific operational actions are regulated by downscaled 7-day weather advisories issued directly by County Directors of Meteorology (CDMs).
Agriculture & Food Security

Crop Production & Post-Harvest Advisory

  • Certified Drought-Tolerant Seeds: Promote dryland cereals (sorghum, finger millet) and pulses (green grams, cowpeas, dolichos lablab) certified by KALRO and state agricultural offices.
  • Moisture Conservation: Deploy in-situ rainwater harvesting techniques including zai pits, tied ridges, and stone contour bunds across agro-pastoral zones.
  • Post-Harvest Protection: If above-normal rains extend into harvest periods, mobilize hermetic storage bags and mobile grain dryers to prevent post-harvest mold and aflatoxin contamination.
Source: KMSA Seasonal Advisory Guidelines (Agriculture Sector) • Ministry of Agriculture & Livestock Development
Pastoralism & Livestock

Rangeland & Animal Health Advisory

  • Strategic Pasture Grazing Reserves: Demarcate dry-season grazing areas and establish fodder banks (hay baling, reseeding of denuded rangelands) ahead of dry spells.
  • Epizootic Disease Surveillance: Flood conditions following severe drought trigger acute outbreaks of mosquito-borne Rift Valley Fever (RVF) and Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia (CCPP). Pre-position ring-vaccination doses.
  • Strategic Commercial De-stocking: During developing drought phases, trigger commercial offtake before animal body condition deteriorates below market exchange thresholds.
Source: KMSA Pastoral Advisory Matrix • Directorate of Veterinary Services • NDMA
Water & Sanitation

Water Infrastructure & Quality Management

  • Dam & Pan Desilting: Desilt earth dams and municipal water pans prior to seasonal rains to maximize volumetric surface capture.
  • Borehole Protection & Water Treatment: Raise borehole wellhead aprons above historical flood lines. Stock community distribution centres with chlorine powder and household water purification sachets.
  • Flood Spillway Reinforcement: Inspect spillways of community water storage structures to prevent breach during high-intensity flash-flood events.
Source: KMSA Water Advisory Protocol • Ministry of Water, Sanitation & Irrigation
Disaster Risk Management

Emergency Contingency & Transport Access

  • Transport Drainage & Culvert Clearing: Clear seasonal storm runoff culverts along primary road corridors and feeder roads before onset to prevent transport severance.
  • County Committee Activation: Convene the County Disaster Management Committee (CDMC) chaired jointly by the County Governor and County Commissioner upon KMSA alert issuance.
  • Community Early Warning: Transmit CDM downscaled advisories in local pastoral languages via vernacular FM radio and NDMA community channels.
Source: KMSA DRM Early Warning Protocols • NDMA Standard Operating Procedures

Official Forecast, Early Warning & Advisory Directory for Kenya

For operational early action triggers, emergency fund disbursements, and statutory disaster declarations, consult Kenya's approved institutions and their operational tools:

Statutory National Authority

Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA)

KMSA (formerly KMD) • Mandated under Meteorology Act No. 7 of 2026

The sole legal authority for meteorological and climate services in Kenya. Formulates, regulates, and issues all official weather forecasts, seasonal climate outlooks, and operational warnings.

Coverage: National (47 Counties)
Cadence: Bi-annual & 7-Day
Operational Tools: Seasonal Climate Outlooks (OND/MAM) • 7-Day County Downscaled Forecasts via County Directors of Meteorology (CDMs) • Severe Weather Advisories

Statutory ASAL Authority

National Drought Management Authority (NDMA)

Mandated under NDMA Act, 2016 • 23 ASAL Counties

Coordinates drought risk management and contingency funding across Kenya's arid and semi-arid lands. Publishes monthly county bulletins establishing official warning stages: Normal, Alert, Alarm, Emergency.

Coverage: 23 ASAL Counties
Cadence: Monthly Early Warning
Operational Tools: Monthly County Early Warning Bulletins • National Drought Emergency Fund (NDEF) Guidelines • Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) System

Section 3.1 • Climate Graphs & Empirical Contingency Distributions — Marsabit

Multi-decadal seasonal precipitation climatology, SPEI-3 drought anomalies, and ocean driver contingency distributions.

🧭 How to Navigate Historical Climate Evidence & Teleconnection Strength

Section 3 provides the empirical bedrock for county climate risk planning. Rather than relying solely on global climate model forecasts, this section catalogs what has actually happened across 44 years of satellite and ocean observations (1981–2024).

1. Questions Answered:
  • How dependable is the ENSO / IOD teleconnection in this specific county?
  • What are the empirical odds of a Wetter vs. Drier season during an El Niño or +IOD?
  • Which sub-counties face severe 100-year riverine flood exposure?
2. Reading Sequence:
  1. Fig 3.1: Multi-decadal rainfall & SPEI-3 anomaly history.
  2. Fig 3.2: Empirical contingency probabilities (tercile odds).
  3. Fig 3.3: Candidate driver regression & correlation ranking.
  4. Fig 3.4 & 3.5: High-resolution spatial raster grids & flood exposure.
3. Physical Limits & Caveats:
  • Non-stationarity: Past frequencies may shift under greenhouse warming.
  • Orographic satellite underestimation around isolated mountain massifs.
  • SAR blindspots: Sentinel-1 orbital passes miss brief flash flood events.
Figure 3.1

Multi-Decadal Precipitation Climatology & Standardized Anomalies (CHIRPS v3 & SPEI-3)

Historical seasonal rainfall and SPEI-3 anomaly time series (1981–2024) with ocean teleconnection markers.

Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Spatial Continuity Rationale

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Ground-based meteorological stations in northern Kenya are extremely sparse—often fewer than one active, reliable rain gauge per 20,000 km². Relying purely on physical weather stations creates massive blind spots across ASAL pastoral rangelands. CHIRPS v3 (UCSB/CHC) blends cold-cloud duration satellite infrared with reporting stations to create continuous 5 km grids spanning 1981 to present. Satellite-gauge blending is the physically grounded standard to track pixel-level subcounty drought and flood anomalies continuously across Kenya.

Key Assumptions
  • WMO Climatological Baseline: Anomalies are computed against the 1991–2020 normal period (30 years) to conform to WMO standard reference rules.
  • Linear Detrending: Long-term greenhouse gas warming trends are detrended before calculating ENSO/IOD teleconnection correlations to isolate interannual ocean forcing.
  • Fixed Accumulation Windows: OND (Oct 1 – Dec 31) and MAM (Mar 1 – May 31) are treated as rigid seasonal boundaries matching agricultural calendars.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Orographic Underestimation: Thermal infrared satellite estimates systematically underestimate localized orographic rainfall around isolated mountain massifs (e.g. Mt. Marsabit, Mt. Kulal).
  • SPEI Evapotranspiration: SPEI-3 utilizes Hargreaves-Samani PET, which can over-estimate evaporative demand during hyper-thermal arid spells.
Primary Source: CHIRPS v3 (0.05°) • Vicente-Serrano SPEI-3 • s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=precipitation/source=chirps-v3/
Figure 3.2

Empirical Contingency Probability Matrix (Tercile Likelihood given Ocean Driver Strength)

Observed conditional probabilities of Wetter, Near-normal, or Drier seasons conditioned on ENSO, IOD, and Western-V intensity classes (1981–2024 record).

How to Read Tercile Probabilities: Historical seasons are stratified into equal thirds based on 1991–2020 climatology: Wetter (top 33.3%), Near-normal (middle 33.3%), and Drier (bottom 33.3%). Under random chance or neutral ocean conditions, each tercile has an unconditional base rate of ~33%. Shifts away from 33% quantify the empirical teleconnection strength.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Non-Parametric Teleconnection Evidence

Honest Physical Limits: Standard linear correlation models oversimplify East African climate teleconnections because rainfall responses are asymmetric and non-linear. The empirical contingency matrix stratifies the historical 44-year record into discrete ocean driver intensity bands (Strong, Moderate, Neutral/Weak) and computes the exact empirical tercile distribution (Wetter / Near-normal / Drier) for each state. This gives planners non-parametric, physically transparent probabilities directly matching KMD 3-tier seasonal forecasts.

Key Assumptions
  • Tercile Climatological Equal-Likelihood: Under climatology, each tercile (Wet, Near, Dry) has an unconditional base rate of 33.3% over the 1991–2020 normal period.
  • Small-Sample Transparency: Groups with fewer than 4 historical seasons are explicitly flagged with an asterisk (*) to warn against interpreting isolated anecdotes as statistical proof.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Sample Size Constraints: Super El Niño and Super +IOD events are rare extremes (n = 3–5 events in 44 years), limiting sample sizes for extreme composite bins.
  • MAM Driver Independence: The Western-V gradient partially decouples from equatorial Pacific ENSO during the Long Rains (MAM), reflecting subtropical Western North Pacific wave trains.
Primary Source: NOAA CPC ONI • HadISST / ERSST DMI • CHIRPS v3 Terciles • s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=indices/
Figure 3.3

How Strongly Do Equatorial Ocean Temperatures Govern County Rainfall?

Candidate ocean driver comparison table, continuous bivariate scatter distribution, and linear regression across all 44 historical seasons (1981–2024).

Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Continuous Teleconnection Sensitivity

Bridging Discrete Bins to Continuous Sensitivity: While contingency matrices (Figure 3.2) group ocean drivers into coarse categorical bins, climate finance proposal writers and disaster contingency planners require exact marginal response metrics: for every +0.5°C or +1.0°C rise in equatorial Pacific SST (RONI) or Western Indian Ocean SST (DMI), how many additional millimetres or percentage points of rainfall are expected? This continuous scatter plot and ordinary least squares (OLS) regression line across all 44 historical years (1981–2024) provides the empirical slope, Pearson correlation coefficient (r), coefficient of determination (R²), and two-tailed p-value.

Key Assumptions
  • Climatological Normal: Anomalies are computed against the WMO standard 1991–2020 reference period.
  • Linear Bivariate Modeling: OLS regression provides the linear teleconnection slope. Non-linear saturation effects during super-events (e.g. 1997, 2023) are visible as residual scatters from the trendline.
  • Seasonal Alignment: OND rainfall is paired with OND ocean indices; MAM rainfall is paired with MAM ocean indices (Western-V / WNP).
Caveats & Statistical Power
  • Collinearity: ENSO and the Indian Ocean Dipole often co-occur during OND (e.g. positive IOD + El Niño in 1997, 2006, 2019, 2023). Raw bivariate r reflects combined ocean basin influence; check the candidate table for multi-driver variance.
  • Outlier Leverage: Extreme years like 1997 and 2023 exert leverage on the slope; points are explicitly labeled to inspect leverage.
Primary Sources: NOAA CPC ONI • HadISST DMI • CHIRPS v3 • data/KE-enso-explorer/chirps_county.parquet

Section 3.2 • Gridded Satellite Climate History & Flood Diagnostics — Marsabit

High-resolution pixel-by-pixel spatial raster maps across historical seasons and hydrodynamic flood exposure benchmarks.

Figure 3.4

Multi-Decadal Gridded Field History & Spatial Patterns (Per-Year Field Canvas Grid)

High-resolution pixel-by-pixel spatial raster maps (CHIRPS v3, SPEI-3, MODIS NDVI, Copernicus GFM Flood, FEWS WRSI) across historical years, tinted by ocean teleconnection state.

Why Pixel-by-Pixel Verification Matters: County-level spatial averages mask extreme local gradients across Kenya's complex topography. By inspecting per-year gridded rasters across independent earth observation systems (CHIRPS v3 rainfall, SPEI-3 drought index, MODIS NDVI vegetation health, Copernicus GFM SAR satellite flood extent, and FEWS/USGS WRSI crop-water satisfaction), proposal teams and disaster managers can verify whether a regional teleconnection anomaly (e.g. 1997 or 2023 El Niño) penetrated into specific pastoral subcounties, grazing corridors, or highland agricultural zones.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Module A: Plot Capabilities & Visual Interpretation
  • Per-Year Facet Canvas: Renders 40+ years of high-resolution gridded satellite observations in an interactive multi-column grid, clipped to official IEBC county boundaries.
  • Ocean Teleconnection Tint: Each year card is subtly tinted by the standardized anomaly (z-score) of the selected oceanic driver (PRGn diverging palette by default: green for wet teleconnection states, purple for suppressing dry states).
  • Anomaly vs. Climatology: Rainfall displays standardized departure from the WMO 1991–2020 reference normal by default (±300 mm scale), isolating true teleconnection impacts from baseline aridity.
  • Multi-Sensor Diagnostics: Switch between 5 earth observation systems to evaluate whether atmospheric moisture translated into surface drought (SPEI-3), vegetation biomass (NDVI), inundation (GFM), or crop satisfaction (WRSI).
Module B: Assumptions, Limitations & Caveats
  • Reference Climatology Baseline: Rainfall anomalies are computed against 1991–2020 WMO standard normal. SPEI-3 is already standard-normalized; MODIS NDVI and Copernicus GFM do not have 30-year baselines.
  • Copernicus GFM Record Length & SAR Masking: Sentinel-1 SAR flood coverage spans only 2018–2025. It reflects recent flood-proneness and orbital pass timing, NOT long-term return-period magnitude. Value 255 (unobserved swath) is strictly excluded as NoData, never counted as dry.
  • HTTP Range COG Streaming: GeoTIFF rasters are window-read on the fly via HTTP range requests against AWS S3 CloudFront, fetching only the county bounding box to preserve client memory.
Module C: Methods & Analysis Summary
  • Driver Independence (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell): Correlation chips display bivariate Pearson r alongside partial correlation (controlling for other drivers) to eliminate double-counting of collinear ENSO and IOD signals.
  • Multi-Driver Linear Combination: Ordinary least squares (OLS) regression calculates the optimal multi-driver variance explained (adjusted R²), identifying whether joint monitoring beats single indices.
  • Phase Intensity Gating: Categorical intensity presets filter analogue historical seasons at |z| ≥ 1.0σ (moderate) and |z| ≥ 1.5σ (strong/extreme) thresholds.

Figure 3.5

Sub-County Flood Inundation & Infrastructure Exposure Explorer

Interactive flood exposure reconciling Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR satellite observations and EC JRC GloFAS 10- to 500-year hydrodynamic flood return periods.

Why Reconciling Satellite & Hydrodynamic Modeling Matters: While satellite radar (SAR) observes individual historical flood footprints, it cannot establish return-period probabilities before disasters occur. The European Commission Joint Research Centre (EC JRC) GloFAS-Hazard v4.0 dataset provides 90 m hydrodynamic modeling derived from 2D LISFLOOD channel simulations (1979–2022). Toggling between observed footprints (2018–2025) and modelled probabilistic benchmarks gives planners a complete picture of contingent vulnerability.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Module A: Plot Capabilities & Visual Interpretation
  • Dual-Source Diagnostics: Toggle between observed satellite radar footprints (Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR) and modelled probabilistic benchmarks (EC JRC GloFAS 10- to 500-year return periods).
  • Multi-Scenario Comparison: Select multiple return period checkboxes (10 to 500 years) to compare the non-linear expansion of inundated territory against built infrastructure.
  • Population Denominators: Headcounts reflect official KNBS 2019 National Census totals distributed across WorldPop 100 m residential building footprints.
Module B: Assumptions, Limitations & Caveats
  • HOT-OSM Volunteer Gaps: Health center and school locations originate from crowdsourced Humanitarian OpenStreetMap (HOT-OSM). In remote pastoral counties, crowdsourced coverage is incomplete. A value of zero exposed schools reflects absence of volunteer mapped points, NOT immunity to floods.
  • Riverine vs. Flash Floods: GloFAS models riverine overtopping along major channel networks (Tana, Ewaso Ng'iro, Daua). It does not capture sudden convective cloudbursts flushing through dry sand-rivers (laggas / wadis).
  • Stationarity Assumption: Return periods assume stationary hydrologic extremes over the 1979–2022 reanalysis window; intensifying warming may shift 100-year events into 50-year frequencies.
Module C: Methods & Analysis Summary
  • Hydrodynamic Routing: 2D LISFLOOD hydrological model forced by GloFAS runoff, routing peak discharge through digital elevation models to compute water depth rasters.
  • Spatial Exposure Intersect: Performed via DuckDB spatial polygon-in-raster operations, clipping depth surfaces at ≥ 0.15 m threshold across subcounty boundaries.
  • Seasonal Asymmetry: OND floods are basin-wide riverine surges driven by El Niño and +IOD; MAM floods are localized flash floods driven by Western-V convective cloudbursts.

4 Historical Impacts • Multi-Sector Vulnerability

Section 4 • Historical Impacts & Multi-Sector Vulnerability — Marsabit

Quantifying how Pacific and Indian Ocean warming signals propagate through subnational crop yields, pastoral herd demography, market terms of trade, and hydrodynamic flood exposure.

How to Navigate Historical Impacts & Vulnerability: Causal Attribution vs. Statistical Association

Section 3 established the multi-decadal meteorological patterns of rainfall and drought. Section 4 traces the consequential chain of real-world outcomes across four socioeconomic and biophysical domains:

4 Sector Pathways
1. Bimodal Crop & Livestock Balances

HarvestStat & KNBS NAPR audited series. In Kenya's bimodal system, annual agricultural output combines preceding Short Rains (OND) and concurrent Long Rains (MAM). Livestock herd mortality exhibits a 6–12 month biological lag following severe pasture droughts.

2. Pasture Biomass & Market Terms of Trade

864 dekads of MODIS NDVI track continuous rangeland forage flushes and deficits. FEWS NET market prices evaluate Terms of Trade (ToT): the kilograms of maize purchased by selling 1 medium goat, pinpointing acute economic distress.

3. Hydrodynamic Flood & Asset Exposure

Downstream exposure of populations, road networks, health facilities, schools, and electrical grids intersected with Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR observed inundation and EC JRC GloFAS return periods.

4. Humanitarian Emergency Chronology

UN OCHA ReliefWeb disaster situation reports (2010–2026). Tracks official flash appeals, disaster declarations, and institutional relief mobilization across historical famine and deluge epochs.

Core Project Guidance — Association is Not Causation: Equatorial ocean indices alter the conditional probability distribution of seasonal rainfall, but local socioeconomic impacts are mediated by soil moisture memory, seed access, animal vaccination, road transport accessibility, and early humanitarian financing. An El Niño warming increases wet-season odds, but realized crop yields depend on agronomic management and pest dynamics.
Figure 4.1

Dual-Season Ocean Drivers vs. Agricultural & Livestock Output — Marsabit

Linking the bimodal climate signal (MAM Long Rains + OND Short Rains) to KNBS county agricultural production statistics and livestock outputs (2016–2024).

The Bimodal Agricultural Attribution Reality: In Kenya's bimodal climate, annual crop production reported by KNBS is the composite result of two distinct seasonal harvests: the MAM Long Rains (planted Mar, harvested Jul/Aug, steered by the Western-V) and the OND Short Rains (planted Oct, harvested Jan/Feb of the following year, steered by IOD and ENSO). Single-season climate shocks can often be absorbed, but consecutive failures across both seasons trigger systemic collapse.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Official Subnational Series

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Subnational agricultural statistics in Kenya have historically been fragmented. We combine the official KNBS National Agricultural Production Reports (2019–2024) with HarvestStat Africa v1.2 (1965–2024, Lee et al. 2025, Nature Scientific Data) to construct the first continuous, audited multi-decadal production series linked directly to ocean driver indices.

Key Assumptions
  • 5-Year Rolling Climatological Baseline: Harvest anomalies are calculated relative to the preceding 5-year rolling median to account for gradual expansion in cultivated acreage.
  • Lagged Harvest Accounting: OND Short Rains crops are planted in October and harvested in January/February of year t+1; this physical lag is explicitly harmonized in the annual statistics.
Caveats & Limitations
  • ASAL Arid Zone Bias: In Marsabit, rainfed maize is cultivated almost exclusively on high-elevation microclimates (Mt. Marsabit and Moyale bluffs). Rangeland livestock output represents 95% of agricultural asset value.
  • Cross-Edition Discrepancies: KNBS 2023-24 vs 2024-25 editions exhibit slight rebasings (median ratio 0.96); numbers are locked to latest published KNBS revisions.
Primary Sources: KNBS NAPR (2019–2024) • HarvestStat Africa v1.2 • CHIRPS v3 • MODIS MOD13Q1
Figure 4.2

Empirical Ocean Driver Phase Response vs. Mean Output — Marsabit

Evaluating observed range intervals, sample sizes, and average agricultural outputs conditioned on categorical ocean teleconnection states (KNBS audited survey years).

National Harvest-Aligned Attribution Convention: Production years are aligned to the seasons harvested within them: OND of the previous year (t−1) plus MAM of the reporting year (t). KNBS does not publish its own convention; this alignment was selected by testing county maize yields against candidate season mappings (2019–2024). Short-rains drivers (ENSO, IOD) evaluate the state at OND(t−1); Long-rains drivers (Western-V) evaluate at MAM(t).
Note on Eastern Counties: In short-rains dominant counties (Tana River, Meru, Kitui, Makueni), OND of the reporting year (t) is the primary driver (r = 0.40) while MAM is negligible.
Figure 4.3

Continuous MODIS Dekadal NDVI Pasture Biomass Dynamics (2002–2026) — Marsabit

Pixel-weighted MODIS NDVI series (864 dekads spanning 2002–2026) across Marsabit County. Values below 100% indicate vegetative drought stress and rangeland forage deficits.

Figure 4.4

Pastoral Market Prices & Terms of Trade (ToT) Monthly Purchasing Power — Marsabit

Monthly retail food and livestock prices monitored across sentinel markets in Marsabit County (FEWS NET Data Warehouse). Evaluating purchasing power collapses during acute drought crises.

Terms of Trade (ToT) Economic Formulation: Quantifies pastoral purchasing power as the kilograms of white maize grain purchased by selling one medium live goat:
ToT (kg maize / goat) = Retail Goat Price (KES / head) ÷ Retail Maize Grain Price (KES / kg)
In normal years across Marsabit, 1 goat purchases 65–75 kg of maize grain. During severe droughts, grazing collapses force distress livestock dumping (depressing goat prices), while grain prices soar. When ToT falls below the 25 kg/goat emergency threshold, pastoral households experience catastrophic purchasing power collapse.

Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Causal Transmission Mechanism

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Meteorological drought does not directly starve people; the market terms of trade do. The FEWS NET Data Warehouse (USAID) provides monthly retail and wholesale price monitoring across sentinel markets in 42 counties (2000–2026). This connects oceanic temperature anomalies directly to pastoral household purchasing power and acute hunger.

Key Assumptions
  • Mandatory Detrending: Nominal Kenyan Shilling prices are deflated using national CPI and detrended to isolate climate shock spikes.
  • Terms-of-Trade (ToT) Ratio — derived, not sourced: Quantifies the purchasing power of pastoralists as the kilograms of maize grain purchased by the sale of one medium live goat. We compute it here as goat price ÷ maize price from the FEWS NET series; no agency publishes it. Being a ratio, a fall can mean either cheaper livestock or dearer grain — opposite implications for a herder — so read it alongside the two price legs above, never alone.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Sentinel Market Bias: Prices are recorded in primary subcounty hubs (Marsabit Town, Moyale, North Horr); remote nomadic camps face substantial unrecorded transport markups.
  • Cross-Border Trade Flows: Unofficial livestock inflows from southern Ethiopia during regional crises can depress local livestock prices independently of Marsabit rainfall.
  • Food Insecurity Benchmark & Licence (CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO): Official IPC acute food insecurity phases (Phases 1–5) and humanitarian caseload numbers are published by the IPC Global Support Unit and Kenya Food Security Steering Group (KFSSG). In accordance with CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO, IPC data are presented strictly for non-commercial reference and cited verbatim; they are never blended or merged into CC-BY-4.0 derived analytical layers.
Primary Sources: FEWS NET Data Warehouse retail prices • MODIS MOD13Q1 • IPC Acute Food Insecurity (CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO). Terms of Trade derived here from the FEWS price series.

Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Operational Radar Physics

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Optical satellite sensors are completely blinded by heavy convective storm clouds during flood crises. Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR is the sole operational sensor emitting microwave radar pulses to penetrate cloud cover and map open water at ~111 m. Intersecting with official KNBS 2019 Census counts (and 2020–2045 projections) distributed by WorldPop 100m building footprint shares provides the ground-truth count of exposed populations.

Key Assumptions
  • Census-Anchored Spatial Distribution: Population totals are calibrated to official KNBS 2019 Census levels (and KNBS annual projections for post-2020 events), distributed proportionally across sub-counties using WorldPop 100 m building footprints.
  • Year-Matched Denominators: Observed flood events are matched against the population denominator of their respective flood year (multi-year sums mix population vintages).
  • Maximum Seasonal Footprint: Observed extents represent the seasonal composite union of all inundation detected across Sentinel-1 orbital passes.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Orbital Revisit Gaps (Blank ≠ Zero): Sentinel-1 revisit interval is 6–12 days; flash floods cresting and draining within 24h between passes are not recorded.
  • Radar Mask Value 255: Denotes unobserved radar shadow or permanent water—never dry land.
Primary Source: Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR • KNBS 2019 Census & Projections (WorldPop 100m share) • s3://digital-atlas/domain=exposure/type=intersect/region=kenya/processing=analysis-ready/

Why this data & analysis? Humanitarian Ground-Truthing

Ground-Truthing Climate Anomalies: Meteorological indices and satellite NDVI monitor physical environmental departures, but UN OCHA ReliefWeb situation reports capture the humanitarian institutional response—documenting when local coping capacities broke down, official government disaster declarations were issued, and international appeals were launched.

Key Tagging Rules
  • First-Match Classification Hierarchy: Reports tagged with multiple simultaneous hazards are classified deterministically in order of priority: Drought → Flood → Epidemic → Other. For example, compound drought and flood reports are counted under Drought.
  • County Matching: Reports are matched to the selected county based on normalized administrative tags, ensuring zero empty counties.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Reporting Attention vs. Hazard Severity: Report volume measures reporting volume, donor visibility, and agency footprint—not physical severity alone. High report counts reflect active emergency appeals and media cycles.
  • Snapshot Vintage: The dataset represents a verified snapshot harvested via the ReliefWeb API spanning January 2010 through June 2026.
Primary Sources: UN OCHA ReliefWeb (reliefweb.int API, 15,736 county-tagged reports across all 47 counties).
Physical Teleconnections & Analytical Foundations

How Equatorial Ocean Dynamics Govern Kenya's Rainfall and Agricultural Vulnerability

An empirical and physical analysis of planetary atmospheric wave dynamics, ocean heat transport, and regional microclimates governing the October–December (Short Rains) and March–May (Long Rains) seasons across Kenya's 47 counties.

Analytical view:
Section 01 • Atmospheric Teleconnections

Theoretical Framework 5.1 • Physical Teleconnection Mechanics: The Pacific-to-Kenya Teleconnection & Equatorial Asymmetry

Kenya is located more than 12,000 kilometers from the equatorial Pacific Ocean. The climatic link between Pacific sea-surface temperature anomalies and rainfall in Marsabit, Garissa, or Kilifi is therefore not mediated by ocean currents, but by planetary-scale shifts in atmospheric circulation cells.

During an El Niño, above-average sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific enhance deep convective thunderstorm formation, shifting the upward ascending limb of the global Walker circulation eastward. In compensatory response, an anomalous ascending cell develops over the western Indian Ocean, drawing moist maritime air over Kenya.

Implication for County Contingency Planning: Because teleconnections operate through statistical shifts in atmospheric circulation rather than deterministic local triggers, El Niño elevates the probability of extreme precipitation events rather than guaranteeing rain on any specific calendar day. Anticipatory disaster risk financing must account for this probabilistic distribution rather than assuming uniform daily rainfall.

The teleconnection between the equatorial Pacific Ocean and the East African plateau is governed by the Walker Circulation—the zonal atmospheric overturning cell driven by equatorial baroclinic pressure gradients.

ΔΩ = −∫p0pt (∇ • vχ) g−1 dp
Where vχ represents the divergent component of upper-tropospheric wind velocity at 200 hPa, g is gravitational acceleration, and p is pressure. Eastward displacement of the convective centroid induces anomalous upper-level divergence over the central Pacific, balanced by an anomalous ascending branch over the western Indian Ocean (50°E–70°E) that lowers regional surface pressure and enhances low-level moisture convergence.
Key References: Hastenrath, S. et al. (2004) Journal of Climate; Webster, P. J. & Yang, S. (1992) Q.J.R. Meteorol. Soc.; Gill, A. E. (1980) Q.J.R. Meteorol. Soc.
Section 02 • Regional Ocean Forcing

Theoretical Framework 5.2 • Regional Ocean Forcing: Indian Ocean Dipole Dominance, Coastal Dynamics & External Benchmarks

While global media coverage focuses heavily on Pacific El Niño events, subnational rainfall in Kenya during the October–December (OND) Short Rains is statistically and physically governed by the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD). The IOD represents anomalous east-west sea temperature contrasts within the Indian Ocean basin directly adjacent to East Africa.

When the western Indian Ocean warms relative to the eastern basin (+IOD), easterly trade winds weaken or reverse, funneling high concentrations of precipitable water directly into Kenya. A modest positive anomaly in the western Indian Ocean (+0.5 °C) routinely generates far more severe flooding in northern and eastern Kenya than a massive Pacific El Niño. This explains why catastrophic inundations occurred in 2019 despite a neutral Pacific state.

Along Kenya's coastal maritime strip (Kwale, Kilifi, Mombasa, Lamu), local sea-surface temperature anomalies and shallow boundary layer moisture fluxes interact directly with large-scale winds. As demonstrated by Gamoyo, Reason & Obura (2015), warm coastal waters can enhance localized convective showers even during moderate regional forcing.

Scope Caveat (Gamoyo et al., 2015): Gamoyo, Reason & Obura (2015) evaluated coastal Kenya and northeastern Tanzania across two specific diagnostic OND seasons (the 1997 extreme wet and 1998 dry events). While foundational for coastal maritime dynamics, these findings represent supporting local context and cannot be extrapolated universally to inland ASALs or the western highlands where continental topography, the Turkana low-level jet, and Lake Victoria basin dynamics govern precipitation.
Off-Diagonal Warning: When the Pacific and Indian Oceans diverge in sign—such as an El Niño occurring alongside a Negative IOD—the two oceanic drivers work in direct opposition. In northern Kenya, the drying effect of a negative Indian Ocean Dipole historically overrides El Niño, creating severe drought risk rather than flood risk.

External Research Comparator: For broader regional perspectives across the Greater Horn of Africa, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) operates the IWMI ENSO Dashboard (and enso.iwmi.org), providing basin-level drought and water balance insights. The Kenya ENSO Explorer coordinates with these regional resources while maintaining independent, audited in-repo CDH GeoParquet pipelines and statutory Republic of Kenya alignments.

The Dipole Mode Index (DMI), formalized by Saji et al. (1999), quantifies anomalous zonal sea-surface temperature gradients across the equatorial Indian Ocean:

DMI(t) = SSTAwest(50°E–70°E, 10°S–10°N) − SSTAeast(90°E–110°E, 10°S–0°)
Partial correlation analysis across Kenya OND precipitation (1981–2025) demonstrates the dominant control of regional Indian Ocean SSTs when controlling for Pacific ENSO:
• Partial correlation r(POND, IOD | ENSO) = +0.72 (p < 0.001, highly significant across ASALs).
• Partial correlation r(POND, ENSO | IOD) = +0.14 (statistically non-significant across northern Kenya).

Gamoyo, Reason & Obura (2015) utilized high-resolution Regional Climate Modeling (WRF) at 15 km grid resolution to isolate the relative contributions of large-scale Indian Ocean SST forcing versus local coastal SST anomalies along the Kenyan coast:

Fmoisture = −∇ • (v q) = − [ ∂(u q)/∂x + ∂(v q)/∂y ]
Where v is horizontal wind velocity and q is specific humidity. Gamoyo et al. demonstrated that onshore moisture convergence Fmoisture is maximized when warm western Indian Ocean anomalies co-occur with anomalously warm localized coastal water, but suppressed during offshore wind regimes.
Caveat: Validated exclusively across coastal Kenya/Tanzania (0°–10°S, 38°–42°E) during OND 1997 and 1998; cannot be applied to inland plateau or Rift Valley domains.
Key References: Saji, N. H. et al. (1999) Nature, 401(6751); Gamoyo, M., Reason, C. J. C., & Obura, D. (2015) Theor. Appl. Climatol., 120; Marchant, R. et al. (2007) Int. J. Climatology; Clark, C. O. et al. (2003) J. Climate.
Section 03 • Climatological Baselines

Table 5.1 • Oceanic & Atmospheric Teleconnection Modes: Why RONI Replaces Traditional Niño 3.4

Public weather bulletins often quote unadjusted Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) numbers (e.g., +1.4 °C or +2.0 °C), while this platform reports NOAA CPC Relative ONI (RONI) at lower values (e.g., +0.88 °C). This adjustment is essential for accurate climate risk evaluation.

Over the last 50 years, global greenhouse warming has elevated the average temperature of all tropical oceans by approximately 0.6 °C. Atmospheric winds and cloud systems do not respond to uniform global warming; they are driven exclusively by temperature contrasts between different ocean basins. Traditional Niño 3.4 conflates global warming with active El Niño dynamics. Standardizing on RONI subtracts the rising tropical background baseline, isolating the true thermal contrast driving weather.

Proposal Integrity Benefit: Relying on unadjusted Niño 3.4 numbers exaggerates modern El Niño frequency and magnitude. Using RONI ensures that adaptation funding proposals and disaster contingency plans are anchored in physically honest, non-inflated climate drivers.

Under anthropogenic warming, spatially uniform SST increases elevate absolute anomalies without inducing baroclinic circulation. Atmospheric convective overturning is governed by horizontal pressure gradients produced by spatial SST gradients (∇SST), requiring removal of the tropical-mean thermodynamic trend.

RONI(t) = ONI(t) − μtropics(t),    where μtropics(t) = ⟨SSTA(20°S–20°N, global)⟩
Because μtropics has trended upward (+0.5 °C since 1980), unadjusted ONI artificially elevates positive anomalies in recent decades. The divergence between RONI and Niño 3.4 has widened from +0.20 °C in the 1980s to −0.30 °C in the 2020s (reaching −0.57 °C during 2024). Standardizing on CPC RONI maintains strict physical consistency between observed index values and dynamical model state probabilities.
Key References: van Oldenborgh, G. J. et al. (2021) BAMS; Vecchi, G. A. & Soden, B. J. (2007) Journal of Climate, 20(17).
Section 04 • Seasonal Asymmetry

Table 5.2 • Seasonal Teleconnection Asymmetry: OND Short Rains vs. MAM Long Rains & Western-V

A common misconception in seasonal planning is assuming that if an El Niño causes heavy rains in October–December, it will persist and cause heavy rains during the March–May (MAM) Long Rains. This assumption is scientifically invalid.

In boreal spring (March–May), Pacific ocean persistence collapses due to the equatorial "Spring Predictability Barrier." Pacific ENSO indices exhibit virtually zero statistical correlation (r ≈ 0.08) with Kenya's Long Rains. MAM rainfall is instead steered by sea-surface temperature gradients in the western Pacific warm pool, known as the Western-V. When this pool warms, it triggers localized convection that forces dry, descending air over East Africa, explaining the persistent Long Rains droughts observed between 1999 and 2022.

Operational Governance: County disaster management directors must decouple OND Short Rains flood response from MAM planning. MAM seasonal forecasts must rely strictly on official seasonal issuances from the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA; formerly KMD) under the Meteorology Act No. 7 of 2026 rather than international media headlines.

The seasonal transition in boreal spring experiences rapid decoupling of tropical boundary-layer anomalies from atmospheric response (Webster & Yang, 1992). The correlation between Kenya MAM precipitation and Niño 3.4 is statistically indistinguishable from zero (r = +0.08, p > 0.50).

WNPstd = [ SSTA(120°E–160°E, 0°–20°N) − μclim ] / σclim
Documented by Funk et al. (2014, 2019, 2023), anomalous warming in the Western North Pacific (WNP) warm pool intensifies deep maritime convection, shifting the ascending branch of regional overturning cells westward and forcing a strong subsiding branch directly over the Horn of Africa during boreal spring. This physical subsidence accounts for the multidecadal suppression of Kenya's Long Rains.
Key References: Funk, C. et al. (2019) BAMS, 100(1); Funk, C. et al. (2014) Climate Dynamics, 42; Hastenrath, S. et al. (2011) Int. J. Climatology.
Section 05 • Scenario Mathematics

Theoretical Framework 5.3 • Forecast Trajectories & Analogue Matching: Curve Shapes vs. Static Seasonal Averages

A standard pitfall in climate communication is reducing an evolving 9-month ocean cycle into a single static number (such as "OND RONI +1.2 °C"). A single seasonal average conceals the temporal velocity, peak timing, and momentum of the ocean-atmosphere system:

• Onset Rate (MJJ → JAS): An ocean state that surges rapidly into positive anomaly territory during May–August primes atmospheric moisture flux and regional trade wind reversals far earlier than a late-blooming event.
• Peak Alignment (OND): If the peak anomaly aligns directly with the southward passage of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) over Kenya in October–November, severe flooding odds are maximized. Conversely, an anomaly peaking late in December delivers its maximum forcing after the Short Rains have already wound down.
• Decay Rate (JFM): How swiftly the anomaly collapses into the subsequent January–March dry season dictates whether secondary pastoral pasture recovery occurs or if acute dry conditions persist into the Long Rains.
• Ensemble Spread & Uncertainty Envelope: Dynamical forecasts from NOAA CPC / IRI are not single deterministic tracks; they are ensemble plumes spanning a 10th-to-90th percentile envelope. Our interface visualizes this full plume envelope alongside operational thresholds (±0.5 °C) so planners see the distribution of plausible trajectories rather than a fabricated single prediction.

To match current conditions against past years, our engine compares multi-month trajectory profiles using statistical standard deviations (z-scores). The Pacific Ocean experiences natural temperature swings more than three times wider than the Indian Ocean (±2.0 °C vs. ±0.4 °C). Without z-score standardization, raw mathematical distance gives the Pacific over ten times more leverage than the Indian Ocean, effectively silencing the Indian Ocean's dominant role in Kenya.

Natural Frequencies over Pseudo-Precision: On small historical samples (e.g., 8 analogue years), claiming "62.5% flood probability" is false precision. We report findings as natural frequencies (e.g., "5 of 8 analogue seasons were wetter than normal") alongside discrete unit indicators to maintain visual and scientific integrity.

Let the ocean trajectory state vector across a temporal evaluation window W be defined as S = [ θt−2, θt−1, θt, θt+1, &dots; ] representing sequential 3-month running anomalies. The dynamic distance between current trajectory 0 and historical candidate season i is computed across both normalized teleconnection axes:

Di = √ [ ∑m∈W ((RONIi,m − RONI0,m) / σRONI,m)2 + ∑m∈W ((DMIi,m − DMI0,m) / σDMI,m)2 ]
In empirical climatology (1981–2025):
• σRONI = 1.179 °C   |   σDMI = 0.362 °C (Variance ratio = 3.25×)
• Raw unstandardized Euclidean distance (ΔRONI2 + ΔDMI2) introduces an artificial leverage distortion of (1.179 / 0.362)2 = 10.6 : 1 in favor of ENSO.
• Standardizing by monthly standard deviation σm ensures equal geometric variance weighting across both ocean basins. Candidate analogues are ranked strictly by ascending distance Di (k-nearest neighbors), entirely eliminating extreme-magnitude bias (sorting by Math.abs).
Key References: Ward, M. N. & Folland, C. K. (1991) Int. J. Climatol.; Drosdowsky, W. (1994) Monthly Weather Review.
Section 06 • Observational Remote Sensing

Theoretical Framework 5.4 • Satellite Radar Detection & Surface Masking: Sentinel-1 SAR Physics, Revisit Blindspots & Waterbody Exclusions

During severe convective storms, optical satellite sensors (such as Landsat or MODIS) are obstructed by dense cloud cover. The Copernicus Global Flood Monitoring (GFM) service utilizes active Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) aboard the Sentinel-1 satellite constellation, transmitting microwave pulses that penetrate clouds, rain, and night darkness. Smooth open floodwaters reflect the radar pulse away from the sensor like a mirror, appearing as stark black water bodies.

Critical Analytical Limitation (Blank ≠ Zero): Sentinel-1 satellites operate on a 6- to 12-day orbital repeat cycle over equatorial Africa. Flash floods in arid seasonal sand rivers (laggas) frequently crest and recede within 24 to 48 hours. If an inundation event occurs between orbital passes, the radar records no flood signature. An unobserved pixel does not indicate safety or absence of flood damage. Subcounties such as Laisamis (63.9% observed during 2023 OND) had over 36% of their territory in radar blindspots; exposed asset totals must be interpreted as observational baselines, never as absolute ceilings.

Permanent Waterbody & Non-Applicable Area Masking: Permanent open lakes and perennial reservoirs (delineated from HydroLAKES v1.0 and RCMRD 30m Land Cover) are explicitly pre-masked in our processing pipeline. This guarantees that permanent water bodies (e.g., Lake Turkana, Lake Victoria, Lake Naivasha, Lake Baringo) are never conflated with seasonal storm flooding. Furthermore, radar blindspots and no-observation pixels are excluded from the county territory denominator rather than treated as verified dry land.

Statutory Disclosure: In all county exposure tables, we explicitly report the orbital coverage percentage (`observed_pct`) and flag subcounties with revisit gaps exceeding 10% to prevent misleading decision-makers into treating unobserved zones as verified safe areas.

Copernicus GFM processes C-band SAR observations (λ ≈ 5.6 cm, frequency 5.405 GHz) acquired in Interferometric Wide (IW) swath mode. The calibrated backscatter coefficient σ° drops sharply (≤ −18 dB) over specular water surfaces compared to diffuse backscatter (−12 to −6 dB) from rough bare rangeland soil.

GFM Pixel Value ∈ { 0: Valid dry land,   1: Valid seasonal flood,   255: Unobserved / Masked }
Masking Formulation & Denominator Exclusion:
• Valid Land Mask: Mland = Msubcounty \ (MHydroLAKES ∪ MRCMRD_water_30m).
• Observed Flooded Fraction = ∑p ∈ Mland 𝕀(p = 1) / ∑p ∈ Mland 𝕀(p ∈ {0, 1}).
• Orbital Coverage Reliability Index = ∑p ∈ Msubcounty 𝕀(p ∈ {0, 1}) / Total Pixels(Msubcounty).
Pixels with value 255 (radar shadow, steep layover, or unobserved passes) are strictly excluded from both numerator and denominator, preventing false dry land inflation.
Key References: Bauer-Marschallinger, B. et al. (2022) Remote Sensing of Environment; Salamon, P. et al. (2021) Copernicus CEMS Technical Documentation; Messager, M. L. et al. (2016) Nature Communications (HydroLAKES).
Section 07 • Economic Transmission Channels

Theoretical Framework 5.5 • Pastoralist Economics: Terms of Trade (ToT) as the Transmission Mechanism

In pastoral rangeland counties such as Marsabit and Turkana, livestock represents over 90% of agricultural asset value. Climate shocks do not cause severe food insecurity primarily through local crop deficits, but through the catastrophic collapse of market Terms of Trade (ToT).

Pastoralist households sell live animals to purchase staple white maize flour. In a normal season, the sale of one medium goat purchases 65 to 75 kilograms of grain—sufficient to sustain a family for over a month. During a prolonged drought, two adverse market forces occur simultaneously: deteriorating pasture causes livestock emaciation, forcing distress sales and halving goat prices; concurrently, regional grain shortages cause maize prices to double. A single goat purchases as little as 20 kilograms of grain, representing a sudden >65% collapse in household purchasing power.

Temporal Grain • Monthly vs. Annual Analysis: In Marsabit market, the terms of trade collapsed by −68.1% in August 2011 and by −65.4% in February 2023. These acute collapses occur at monthly peak-to-trough resolution. Annual averages (−32% to −37%) smooth out and obscure the critical 90-day starvation window that precipitates acute child malnutrition and famine.

Grounding our economic impact analysis in Amartya Sen's (1981) Entitlement Approach, famine in pastoralist rangelands is driven by the failure of exchange entitlements rather than absolute regional food availability decline (FAD).

ToT(t) = Pgoat(t) [KES / head] / Pmaize(t) [KES / kg] = kg maize / goat
Empirical evaluation across 218 monthly price pairs in Marsabit sentinel market (2008–2026):
• Climatological Normal Baseline: 60 to 75 kg maize per goat.
• 2011 Drought Peak (August 2011): ToT collapsed to 20.5 kg (−68.1% peak-to-trough).
• 2020–2023 Drought Trough (February 2023): ToT collapsed to 21.3 kg (−65.4% peak-to-trough).
Econometric modeling demonstrates that monthly terms of trade degradation leads IPC Phase 3+ headcount surges by 60 to 90 days, providing an objective mathematical trigger for anticipatory cash transfers.

Derived, and a ratio. No agency publishes this series — we compute it from the two FEWS NET price legs above. Both legs move, so a fall in ToT is ambiguous on its own: it can mean livestock got cheaper (distress sales, emaciated stock) or grain got dearer (regional shortage), and the two call for different responses. Always read the ratio against its numerator and denominator.
Key References: Sen, A. (1981) Poverty and Famines: An Essay on Entitlement and Deprivation, Oxford University Press; Little, P. D. et al. (2001) Development and Change, 32(3).
Section 08 • Applied Data Gates

Table 5.3 • Applied Research Spikes & Data Gates: Weather Stations, Agroclimatic Indices & Crop Models

In compliance with our Project Data Integrity Governance and Anti-AI Slop protocols, three exploratory technical spikes were conducted during v3 development. Features that failed rigorous data completeness, spatial representativeness, or independent calibration audits were formally gated rather than rushed into production as pseudo-precision features.

Spike 1 • In-Situ Weather-Station Integration (NOAA GHCN-Daily, ISD & Meteostat)

UI Charting: No-Go (v3) Satellite-Gauge CHIRPS: Go

Audit Findings: Spatial inventory of open meteorological stations across Kenya revealed severe representativeness deficits: only ~10 GHCN-Daily stations and ~28 ISD stations exist nationwide. More than 37 of Kenya's 47 counties have zero functional, open-access daily weather stations. Available stations are heavily clustered at airport runways (e.g., JKI Airport, Moi Intl, Kisumu, Eldoret, Lodwar, Mandera) subject to tarmac microclimates unrepresentative of broader county rural zones. Furthermore, precipitation fields in open Meteostat endpoints show >45% missing records in ASAL counties during critical historical decades.

Formal Gate Decision (D22): Charting in-situ stations in the production UI would mislead county planners by presenting airport readings as county-wide benchmarks. The notebook instead validates and stands behind satellite-gauge blended CHIRPS v3, which integrates all verified Kenyan national rain-gauge records into a spatially continuous, peer-reviewed 0.05° grid (Funk et al., 2015).

Spike 2 • High-Resolution Agroclimatic Indices (AgroClimateAF & AgWise)

UI Integration: No-Go (v3) Research Roadmap: Go (v4)

Audit Findings: Evaluated the AgroClimateAF library (github.com/jemsethio/AgClimateAF_indices) for candidate metrics: rainfall onset date, false start, cessation, length of growing period (LGP), dry spell frequency (consecutive dry days ≥7 d, ≥14 d), and extreme precipitation days (P ≥20 mm). While agronomically compelling, the code currently lacks an automated CI/CD pipeline for reproducible GeoParquet compilation, lacks tests handling Kenya's complex bimodal/unimodal transitions, and the companion domain (agroclimateafrica.com) has unverified long-term availability.

Formal Gate Decision (D23): Retained for v4 research pipeline development. Production v3 remains anchored in fully audited, peer-reviewed CHIRPS v3 precipitation, SPEI-3 meteorological drought, and dekadal Water Requirement Satisfaction Index (WRSI).

Spike 3 • Process-Based Crop Simulation Models (DSSAT, APSIM & AgWise)

Production UI: No-Go (v3) Research Spec: Go

Audit Findings: Evaluated dynamic crop simulation models (e.g., DSSAT CERES-Maize, APSIM) and CGIAR-AgWise planting date/cultivar code (github.com/CGIAR-AgWise). Rigorous scientific integrity dictates that uncalibrated crop simulation models must NEVER be presented to county planners as deterministic yield forecasts. Accurate yield simulation in Kenya requires localized cultivar genetic coefficients, calibrated root-zone soil water profiles (ISRIC SoilGrids / Kenya Soil Survey), verified planting dates, and farm management fertilizer inputs. Fabricating pseudo-yield numbers without field-level ground truth violates project integrity.

Formal Gate Decision (D24): Prohibit display of uncalibrated crop model yield projections in the production notebook. Instead, Section 4 reports empirical agricultural production balance sheets directly from audited KNBS National Agricultural Statistics and KALRO publications.

Section 6.2 • Analysis Methods & Mathematical Formulations

Rigorous mathematical models, statistical transformations, spatial aggregation pipelines, and economic formulations implemented across Sections 1 to 5.

Method 01

Spatial Zonal Aggregation & Waterbody Pre-masking

High-resolution raster fields (5 km CHIRPS v3, 250m MODIS NDVI, 1 km JRC GloFAS, 100m WorldPop) are aggregated to IEBC / OCHA COD-AB Kenya County (ADM1) and Sub-county (ADM2) polygons via area-weighted zonal polygon overlays.

X̄poly = [ ∑i ∈ poly wi • Xi ] / [ ∑i ∈ poly wi ],    where wi = Ai • (1 − Mwater,i)
Permanent Waterbody Pre-masking: Prior to computing terrestrial drought or flood statistics, permanent lakes (Turkana, Victoria, Baringo, Naivasha) and perennial wetlands are pre-masked using HydroLAKES v1.0 and RCMRD 30m Land Cover. This prevents perennial open water from corrupting terrestrial land-surface anomalies.
Method 02

Climatological Baselines & Tercile Partitioning (1991–2020)

Adheres strictly to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) 30-year climatological normal reference period (1991–2020, N = 30) to establish stationary reference means and variance bounds.

Below < Q̂0.333,    Q̂0.333 ≤ Near-Normal ≤ Q̂0.667,    Above > Q̂0.667
Equiprobable Partitioning: Under a Gaussian climatological distribution, tercile boundaries correspond to μ ± 0.4307σ. Natural frequencies (X of Y seasons in tercile) are prioritized over raw percentages to communicate small-sample uncertainty (N = 8 analogues).
Method 03

Linear Detrending & Secular Tropical Warming Adjustment

Unadjusted Niño 3.4 sea-surface temperatures carry a substantial secular anthropogenic warming trend (~+0.6 °C since 1950). Subtraction of the tropical-mean background is required to isolate true Walker circulation overturning.

RONI(t) = SSTANiño 3.4(t) − μtropics(t),    where μtropics(t) = ⟨SSTA(20°S–20°N, global)⟩
Elimination of False El Niño States: Subtracting tropical-mean warming prevents historical cool baselines from registering as permanent artificial El Niño conditions. Similarly, agricultural area and production series are detrended to decouple yield shocks from agronomic expansion.
Method 04

Multi-Month Analogue Nearest-Neighbour Distance Metric

Analogue seasons are identified using multi-month trajectory distance across the ocean state vector from pre-season development (MJJ/JAS) through peak alignment (OND) to decay (JFM).

Di = √ [ ∑m ∈ W wm • ((Tcurr,m − Thist,i,m) / σm)2 ],    W = {MJJ, JAS, SON, OND}
Z-Score Standardization: Normalization by monthly standard deviation σm resolves the 10.6 : 1 variance distortion ratio between Pacific SST anomalies and regional rainfall variations, ensuring balanced physical distance computation.
Method 05

Hydrodynamic Flood Hazard & Asset Exposure Intersection

Distinguishes physical inundation hazard from consequential human asset exposure. Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR observed extents and JRC GloFAS return periods (10–500 yr) are intersected with built assets.

Popexposed = ∑j ∈ subcounty [ 𝕀(Floodj = 1) • WorldPopj • (KNBS_Census2019 / ∑ WorldPop) ]
Radar Blindspot Handling (Blank ≠ Zero): Sentinel-1 SAR mask value 255 (unobserved / radar shadow) is excluded from denominators. Unobserved intervals in flash-flood basins are reported explicitly rather than recorded as false non-flooded terrain.
Method 06

Socioeconomic Terms of Trade (ToT) Purchasing Power

Grounded in Amartya Sen's (1981) Entitlements Approach, tracking the ratio of pastoralist sale proceeds to staple food acquisition costs across FEWS NET sentinel markets.

ToT(t) = Pgoat(t) [KES / head] / Pmaize(t) [KES / kg] = kg maize grain / live medium goat
Emergency Collapse Threshold: When pastoral Terms of Trade collapse below 25 kg maize/goat, households enter acute caloric deficits, leading IPC Phase 3+ emergency declarations by 60 to 90 days.
